In this lesson you will learn about troubleshooting operational amplifier circuits.
INTRODUCTIONM
Although the operational amplifier may function as different types of amplifiers, troubleshooting is the same for each.
In most cases, the Op-amp IC is the most likely component to fail. This requires replacement of the IC as you cannot repair integrated circuits.
Measuring the output and comparing it to the input determines if a problem exists.
Replacing the op-amp and rechecking the circuit verifies that the fault has been corrected.

LESSON MENU
Op-amps have many different functions. When troubleshooting, you must first recognize what type of circuit it is.
DISCUSSION
Inverting and non-inverting amps have only one input. To determine normal operation, compare calculated gain with measured gain.
Inverting amps should produce a negative output for a positive DC applied. If AC is applied, the signal should be inverted.
The measured gain should match your calculated gain within
Difference amps have two inputs and summing amps may have even more. To determine normal operation, compare calculated output with measured output.
For this troubleshooting discussion, summing and difference amps with a gain of one are discussed since it is the most common configuration.
If the output of an operational amplifier is incorrect for the given input(s), check Vcc to ensure correct supply voltage.
Since most op-amps require positive and negative supply voltages, both should be checked with an oscilloscope for correct DC voltage levels.
The operational amplifier is faulted if the output is incorrect and the input(s) and supply voltages check good.
